name: DIM supplement

lead: DIM (3,3'-diindolylmethane) is formed when the body digests indole-3-carbinol from cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli and cabbage, and is sold as a supplement. In acne communities it is used for clearer skin by people with hormonal breakouts.

The idea is that DIM shifts estrogen metabolism and androgen balance, lowering androgen-driven oil. Lab studies report antiestrogenic activity through the aryl hydrocarbon receptor and altered sex hormone metabolism. Human research has focused on cancer and other conditions; no clinical studies of DIM for acne were found.

paras: It is taken as a daily oral capsule, often by people whose breakouts follow a hormonal pattern such as along the jawline or around the menstrual cycle. Users generally wait several weeks to a few months before judging skin changes.

Pure DIM carries skin, eye and respiratory irritation hazard labelling. Because it acts on hormone metabolism, people with hormone-sensitive conditions or who take hormonal medication have reason to check with a clinician first. Long-term effects of supplementation for acne have not been studied in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Used off-label for hormonal acne, DIM is taken to shift estrogen and androgen balance, lowering oil and breakouts. The research on DIM concerns hormones and cancer; acne has not been studied.

lead: 3,3'-Diindolylmethane (DIM) is a compound formed in the stomach when indole-3-carbinol, a breakdown product of glucobrassicin in cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, Brussels sprouts and kale, meets stomach acid.[1][2][3] It is sold over the counter as a dietary supplement and is also available as a component of multi-ingredient 'hormone balance' and 'estrogen management' products.[1][4][5]

People take DIM to look better by two routes. In acne communities the chain is hormonal: nudging estrogen (and, as some dermatologists propose, androgen) signalling is meant to calm oil production and cyclical breakouts, giving clearer skin.[4][6] In bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy circles the chain runs through estrogen management: keeping estrogen-driven water retention, puffiness and gynecomastia-type chest changes in check so the physique looks drier and leaner.[4][5][7][8]

Published research on DIM concerns laboratory biology, hormone metabolism and cancer-related questions rather than skin.[2][9][10] Small human trials have measured estrogen-metabolite ratios, BRCA1 expression, breast density and body fat after DIM supplementation.[11][12][13][14] One dermatologist quoted in Women's Health said there are no randomised placebo-controlled studies of DIM for acne.[6]

paras: DIM is taken orally, usually as a capsule, as a stand-alone supplement or as one ingredient in blends that often include calcium D-glucarate.[1][8] Because it is a product of vegetables, it is described by sellers as a concentrated way to get the effect of cruciferous vegetables.[1]

In acne communities DIM is discussed as a 'hormonal acne' supplement for jawline and cyclical breakouts. Dermatologist Morgan Rabach told Women's Health in 2020 that DIM may act somewhat like spironolactone by occupying androgen receptors in the skin so less oil is produced, a mechanism she presented as plausible rather than proven.[6] She also said individual results vary and that diet, hygiene and stress may override any effect.[6]

On T Nation, DIM appears in threads on managing estradiol and in supplement stacks listed 'to improve estrogen management', often alongside calcium D-glucarate.[4][5][7][8] Users on testosterone therapy discuss it among estrogen-management supplements, and some ask whether clinical findings support a more favourable estrogen profile.[7][15][16] Their stated goal is a leaner, less puffy look and avoidance of estrogen-related breast tissue changes.

Under acidic conditions such as stomach acid, indole-3-carbinol converts to a series of condensation products, of which DIM is a major component, and these are thought to account for many of its biological effects.[2] DIM has the formula C17H14N2.[1] Cruciferous vegetables contain the precursor glucosinolate glucobrassicin, which breaks down into indole-3-carbinol when plant tissue is damaged, and urinary DIM has been studied as a biomarker of glucobrassicin intake.[3][17]

Glucosinolate breakdown products from cruciferous vegetables are reported to alter the metabolism and activity of sex hormones in ways that could inhibit hormone-sensitive cancers, although epidemiological evidence for an inverse association with cancer risk is mixed.[9] A 1998 Carcinogenesis paper described aryl hydrocarbon receptor-mediated antiestrogenic activity of DIM in laboratory models.[10] In vitro, DIM has been reported to inhibit histone deacetylases HDAC1 to HDAC3 and to bind weakly to cannabinoid receptors.[1]

The estrogen-metabolite claim rests on shifting the ratio of 2-hydroxyestrone to 16-alpha-hydroxyestrone, a urinary marker that studies use as a proxy for 'favourable' versus 'less favourable' estrogen breakdown.[11][14] Reviews also describe effects on cancer-stem-cell pathways and epigenetic regulation in cell and animal models.[18][19]

A mouse study examined the pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution of indole-3-carbinol and its acid condensation products after oral dosing.[20] A 2014 trial reported urinary DIM as a biomarker of vegetable intake.[17] In a human micro-dosing study, DIM supplements and Brussels sprouts were compared for effects on how the body handles the environmental compound benzo[a]pyrene.[21]
No studies found for acne or appearance outcomes. The human work that exists addresses estrogen metabolism and cancer-related questions.

Body fat and estrogen metabolites: a randomised, double-blind trial in 60 premenopausal Mexican women with a low urinary estrogen-metabolite ratio gave DIM or placebo for about a month. The authors reported no significant rise in the ratio during supplementation, with a non-significant upward trend afterwards, and a larger fall in body-fat percentage in the DIM group; they called for further work on dose, timing and body-fat effects.[11]

Thyroid disease: in a 2011 phase I pilot, patients with proliferative thyroid disease took DIM for two weeks before surgery. DIM was detected in thyroid tissue, serum and urine, and the 2-hydroxyestrone to 16-alpha-hydroxyestrone ratio rose, which the authors read as an antiestrogenic shift.[14][22]

BRCA1 and breast density: in an 18-woman study, 13 BRCA1 mutation carriers took DIM for four to six weeks and five served as controls; most DIM takers showed higher BRCA1 mRNA in white blood cells, with a borderline-significant average increase of about a third.[12] A separate prospective trial examined DIM and breast density in BRCA carriers.[13]

Other registered or published human studies have looked at breast cancer, prostate cancer, lupus and healthy volunteers; several were small, and some were terminated or withdrawn.[23][24][25][26][27][28][29] A 2023 laboratory study reported that DIM reduced Streptococcus mutans biofilm, and Wikipedia notes that no clinical trials have confirmed an effect on plaque.[1][30]

The chemical's hazard classification lists skin, eye and respiratory irritation for the pure compound.[1] For supplements, Rabach listed nausea, vomiting, bloating, diarrhoea, gas and headaches as the most commonly reported effects, and a naturopathic doctor in the same article noted that DIM metabolites can darken urine.[6] The article also noted that supplements are not verified by the FDA for label accuracy, so actual content can vary.[6] Long-term safety in people using DIM for hormonal acne has not been described in published studies.[6]

DIM is discussed on hormone and bodybuilding forums mainly as a natural way to lower estrogen effects, and in acne circles as a hormonal-acne supplement.[4][5][8][6] Mainstream coverage such as Women's Health has presented it as an option dermatologists are cautious about recommending without trials, and advises consulting a doctor first.[6] Some forum users report relief from other hormone-linked symptoms; one T Nation poster describes a partner saying DIM eased premenstrual mood symptoms.[31]
